children: By Robb M. Stewart and Paul Vieira
OTTAWA--Canadians will continue to see relief at the pumps after Prime Minister Mark Carney's government extended a fuel-tax break until early next year.

The government will continue a temporary suspension of the federal fuel excise tax through the end of January, after which it will apply half of the usual tax from Feb. 1 to March 31. The break, which has been in place since April 20 and had been set to run through Sept. 7, will now end in April.
"This is the most impactful measure we can put together," Finance Minister Francois-Philippe Champagne said at a press conference in Ottawa.
"It is a direct measure . . . no matter where you live in the country," he added.

The move is aimed at keeping more money in Canadians' pockets as the country contends with the disruptions in the Middle East that have pushed up energy costs and a trade war with the U.S. that has heightened uncertainty, Champagne said.

Resilient household spending has underpinned the economy of late, and--alongside a rise in exports and recovery in business investment--helped drive the strongest economic growth in roughly three years during the second quarter. Yet, despite the rise in consumption, households spent less on gasoline in the latest quarter.
The fuel-tax break saves 10 Canadian cents (7.2 U.S. cents) on a liter on gas and 4 Canadian cents a liter on diesel and aviation fuel.
The government estimated extending the fuel excise tax will cost about C$2.9 billion, which would mean C$5.3 billion in tax relief for Canadians in 2026-27.

The move to extend tax relief comes as the economy faces a turbulent autumn, as trade ties with the U.S. deteriorate and President Trump threatens to impose a potentially crippling 50% tariff on Canadian-made motor vehicles and auto parts on Jan. 1.

Trade talks on a new U.S.-Canada agreement broke down suddenly last month, leading the Trump administration to impose a 50% tariff on about US$20 billion of Canadian imports. Canada intends to retaliate with tariffs ranging from 15% to 50% on U.S. goods starting next Tuesday.

When the temporary gas-tax relief was first introduced, Carney said the hope was that energy prices would stabilize by the fall. The U.S. and Iran restarted military attacks this week, and oil prices have climbed to the $90 a barrel level, a roughly 34% increase from the start of the Middle East war.
